{{short description|Mathematical formula used to calculate heritability in twin studies}}
{{Context|date=March 2024}}
[[Heritability]] is the proportion of variance caused by genetic factors of a specific trait in a population.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Ge|first1=Tian|last2=Holmes|first2=Avram J.|last3=Buckner|first3=Randy L.|last4=Smoller|first4=Jordan W.|last5=Sabuncu|first5=Mert R.|date=2017-05-08|title=Heritability analysis with repeat measurements and its application to resting-state functional connectivity|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=114|issue=21|pages=5521–5526|doi=10.1073/pnas.1700765114|pmid=28484032|pmc=5448225|issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free|bibcode=2017PNAS..114.5521G }}</ref> '''Falconer's formula''' is a mathematical [[formula]] that is used in [[Twin study|twin studies]] to estimate the relative contribution of genetic vs. environmental factors to variation in a particular [[Phenotypic trait|trait]] (that is, the heritability of the trait) based on the difference between [[twin]] [[Correlation and dependence|correlations]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Weber |first1=Wendell W. | name-list-style = vanc |title=Pharmacogenetics |date=2008 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-971216-8 |pages=107–8 |edition=2nd | chapter = Chapter 5: Genetics in Pharmacology: Twin Studies | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=xvK8BKbeNWAC&pg=PA107 }}</ref> Statistical models for heritability commonly include an error that will absorb phenotypic variation that cannot be described by genetics when analyzed. These are unique subject-specific influences on a trait.<ref name=":0" /> Falconer's formula was first proposed by the Scottish geneticist [[Douglas Scott Falconer|Douglas Falconer]].<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Falconer DS, Mackay TF | title = Introduction to quantitative genetics | date = 1998 | publisher = Longman Group, Ltd. | location = Essex | isbn = 978-0-582-24302-6 | edition = 4th | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/introductiontoqu00falc }}</ref>

The formula is <math display="block">{H_b}^2 = 2(r_{mz} - r_{dz})</math>
where <math display="inline">{H_b}^2</math> is the broad sense heritability, <math>r_{mz}</math> is the (monozygotic, MZ) [[Twin#Monozygotic_(identical)_twins|identical twin]] correlation, and <math display="inline">r_{dz}</math> is the (dizygotic, DZ) [[Twin#Dizygotic (fraternal) twins|fraternal twin]] correlation. Falconer's formula assumes the equal contribution of environmental factors in MZ pairs and DZ pairs. Therefore, additional phenotypic correlation between the two pairs is due to genetic factors. Subtracting the correlation of the DZ pairs from MZ pairs yields the variance in phenotypes contributed by genetic factors.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mayhew|first1=Alexandra J.|last2=Meyre|first2=David|date=2017-07-26|title=Assessing the Heritability of Complex Traits in Humans: Methodological Challenges and Opportunities|journal=Current Genomics|volume=18|issue=4|pages=332–340|doi=10.2174/1389202918666170307161450|pmid=29081689|issn=1389-2029|pmc=5635617}}</ref> The correlation of same sex MZ twins is always higher than the DZ twin correlation with various sexes and thus all [[gender differences]] are evaluated as heritable. To avoid this error, only genetic studies comparing MZ twins with the same sex DZ twins are valid. Correlations between <math display="inline">A = {H_b}^2</math> (additive genetics) and <math>C</math> (common environment) must be included in the derivation shown below.

<math display="block">r_{mz} = A + C + 2 \cdot \text{Corr}(A,C)</math>
<math display="block">r_{dz} = \frac{1}{2}A + C + 2 \cdot \text{Corr}(\tfrac{1}{2}A,C)</math>
